beer-lambert-law-s1.title: Calibration curve for a blue food dye
beer-lambert-law-s1.text: A student measures five standard solutions of a blue dye at 630 nm in 1.00 cm cuvettes after zeroing the instrument with water. A diluted sports drink gives an absorbance of 0.565.

beer-lambert-law-s2.title: Measuring copper(II) ions
beer-lambert-law-s2.text: Copper(II) solutions absorb strongly at 810 nm. A student measures three samples with a spectrophotometer.

items.q: Use the calibration curve to find the dye concentration in the diluted drink, in units of 10⁻⁵ M (for example, 3.00 means 3.00 × 10⁻⁵ M).

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied the absorbance by the slope. Concentration is A ÷ slope.

why.correct: The line passes through the origin with slope 1.131 / 10.0 = 0.1131 per 10⁻⁵ M. c = 0.565 / 0.1131 = 4.996, so 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ M.

items.q: The slope of the line equals εb. With b = 1.00 cm, what is the molar absorptivity of the dye?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided concentration by absorbance. The slope is ΔA ÷ Δc.

items.q: Before measuring the drink, the student touches the clear faces of its cuvette, leaving fingerprints. How does this affect the concentration she reports?
options: Too high, because the fingerprints absorb or scatter light and raise the absorbance.
Too low, because the fingerprints let more light reach the detector.
No effect, because the fingerprints are outside the cuvette and not in the solution.
Too low, because fingerprints raise the path length b of the cuvette.

why.correct: Any light lost at the cuvette walls is counted as absorbed by the sample. A higher absorbance read on the calibration line gives a higher concentration.
options: Right: extra absorbance, higher concentration.
Fingerprints block or scatter light; they do not let more through.
The beam passes through the walls, so anything on them affects the reading.
Path length is the inside width, which does not change.

items.q: Why are the standards and the drink measured at 630 nm?
options: 630 nm is near λmax, where the reading is most sensitive.
630 nm is where water absorbs most strongly, so the blank cancels the most light.
630 nm is the color of the dye seen by eye, so it is the light that the dye absorbs.
630 nm is the shortest visible wavelength, so its photons carry the most energy.

why.correct: At λmax, ε is largest, so each change in concentration gives the largest change in absorbance, and small wavelength errors matter least.
options: Right: maximum absorbance, maximum sensitivity.
Water absorbs very little visible light; the blank removes small effects.
The dye looks blue because it absorbs orange-red light near 630 nm and transmits blue.
Violet, near 400 nm, is the shortest visible wavelength.

items.q: The drink was diluted by mixing 10.0 mL of it with water to a total of 50.0 mL. What was the dye concentration in the undiluted drink?

why.correct: The diluted solution is 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ M. The dilution factor is 50.0 / 10.0 = 5.00, so the original is 5.00 × 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ M = 2.50 × 10⁻⁴ M (M₁V₁ = M₂V₂).
options: This divides by the dilution factor instead of multiplying.
This is the diluted concentration, not the original.
This used the 40.0 mL of water added as V₁ (50.0/40.0); the volume of drink taken was 10.0 mL.
Right: multiply back by the dilution factor.

items.q: From sample 1, what is the molar absorptivity of copper(II) at 810 nm?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied A by c. Rearrange A = εbc to ε = A/(bc).

why.correct: A is proportional to c. Doubling c from 0.0500 to 0.1000 M doubles A: 2 × 0.592 = 1.184, so 1.18.
options: This halves instead of doubling.
This ignores the change in concentration.
Right: twice the concentration, twice the absorbance.
This quadruples; A is proportional to c, not c².

why.correct: A is proportional to the path length b. Same concentration as sample 1 but twice the path: 2 × 0.592 = 1.18.
options: This divides by 10 for no reason.
A longer path increases A; it does not halve it.
A longer path passes more absorbing ions, so A rises.
Right: twice the path, twice the absorbance.

items.q: The student forgets to zero the instrument with a water blank, and the cuvette and water together absorb 0.015. How are her results affected?
options: Each absorbance is 0.015 too high, so each concentration is too high.
Each absorbance is 0.015 too low, so each concentration she calculates is too low.
The absorbances are unaffected, because water absorbs no light at 810 nm.
The molar absorptivity changes, because ε depends on the volume of water present.

why.correct: Without a blank, the instrument counts light lost to the cuvette and water as absorbed by copper(II). Each reading is too high, and c = A/(εb) is too high.
options: Right: a higher reading means a higher calculated concentration.
Extra absorbing material raises, not lowers, the reading.
The question states the cuvette and water absorb 0.015.
ε is a property of copper(II) at 810 nm; the error is in A.

items.q: A solution of a compound with ε = 6,220 L/(mol·cm) at 340 nm has an absorbance of 0.373 in a 1.00 cm cuvette. What is its concentration?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied A by ε. Rearrange A = εbc to c = A/(εb).
Value: you divided ε by A. Concentration is c = A/(εb).

items.q: In A = εbc, what does b stand for?
options: The path length of light through the sample
The molar absorptivity of the substance
The concentration in mol/L
The wavelength of the light used

why.correct: b is the path length, the distance light travels through the solution, usually 1.00 cm.
options: Right: usually 1.00 cm.
That is ε.
That is c.
The wavelength is chosen (λmax) but is not a variable in the equation.

items.q: Put the steps for finding an unknown concentration with a calibration curve in order.
options: Find λmax by scanning a standard across wavelengths
Zero the spectrophotometer with a blank of the solvent
Measure the absorbance of each standard at λmax
Plot absorbance against concentration and fit a line
Measure the unknown and read its concentration from the line

why.correct: Pick the wavelength, zero with a blank, measure the standards, build the line, then measure the unknown.

items.q: Which errors would make a reported concentration too high? Select all that apply.
options: A water drop on the outside of the cuvette
Skipping the blank when the solvent absorbs slightly
Using a cuvette with a shorter path length than the standards' cuvette
Diluting the unknown more than recorded
Measuring at a wavelength away from λmax for both standards and unknown

why.correct: A drop and a missed blank both add absorbance that is counted as the sample's. A shorter path lowers A, and over-dilution lowers the measured concentration; measuring everything at another wavelength only lowers sensitivity.
options: Right: extra light lost, higher A.
Right: the solvent's absorbance is added to every reading.
A shorter path gives a lower A and so a lower concentration.
Extra unrecorded dilution makes the calculated original concentration too low.
If standards and unknown use the same wavelength, the curve still works, just less sensitively.

items.q: Why does a colorless solution of sugar give an absorbance near zero at 630 nm?
options: Sugar has no energy gap matching 630 nm photons.
Sugar molecules are too small to block light of a visible wavelength.
Sugar molecules absorb 630 nm light but then re-emit it at the same moment.
Sugar solutions are too dilute to absorb any light in a 1.00 cm cuvette.

why.correct: Absorption needs a photon whose energy matches a gap between levels. Sugar has no electronic transitions in the visible, so ε at 630 nm is about zero.
options: Right: ε is near zero at that wavelength.
Size does not decide absorption; matching energy gaps do.
Absorbed energy is mostly turned into heat, and here nothing is absorbed.
Even concentrated sugar solutions are colorless.

items.q: A student's most concentrated standard falls well below the straight line through the other points. Her unknown gives an absorbance above that standard. What should she do?
options: Dilute the unknown by a known factor so its absorbance falls within the straight part of the line, then multiply back.
Read the unknown from a straight line extended past the last standard, since Beer's law holds for any absorbance.
Report the unknown as equal to the most concentrated standard, the highest value the curve reaches.
Measure the unknown at a wavelength far from λmax, where its absorbance reads higher.

why.correct: At high absorbance, readings can fall below the Beer's-law line. Diluting the unknown into the range covered by good standards gives a reliable reading; multiplying by the dilution factor returns the original concentration.
options: Right: stay within the calibrated range.
The curve has already bent at high absorbance, so extending the line is unreliable there.
Its absorbance is higher, so its concentration is likely higher too.
Away from λmax the absorbance is lower, not higher, and the standards were not measured there.

items.q: A dye solution in a 1.00 cm cuvette has A = 0.300 at λmax. Which changes would double its absorbance at λmax? Select all that apply.
options: Doubling the dye concentration
Pouring twice the volume of the same solution into the cuvette
Using a lamp twice as bright
Switching to a 0.50 cm cuvette

why.correct: A = εbc. Only c and b (and ε, fixed for the dye at λmax) change A. Doubling c doubles A; the volume poured in and the brightness of the lamp do not appear in the equation, and a shorter path halves A.
options: Right: A is proportional to c.
The light crosses the same 1.00 cm of solution however much is in the cuvette.
Absorbance is a ratio of light out to light in, so a brighter lamp leaves it unchanged.
Halving the path length halves A.
